text:
Celeriac.
DIFFICULTY
Tricky
4/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Autumn

Celeriac, or turnip-rooted celery, is grown for its swollen stem-base. Its earthy celery flavour suits soups, stews, salads and winter dishes; lifted roots keep into spring if stored cool. It needs less blanching and earthing-up work than celery, but still needs a full season, a good start under cover and rich, moisture-retentive soil. Shallow, fibrous roots suffer in dry ground: water steadily in dry weather. Heavy, well-composted soil suits it well; varieties are broadly similar.

Quick facts
Harvest

Oct – Nov

Germination

12–21 days

Sow indoors

Mar–Apr under cover.

Row spacing

18 in. between rows

Yield (10 ft row)

7 lb

Plant spacing

12 in. between plants

Planting depth

Stem-base level with soil; keep crown clear.

Ready in

About 30–35 weeks from sowing

Plant out

May–Jun after late frosts.

Recommended varieties
Prinz

A dependable celeriac for rounded roots and useful kitchen quality. A strong first choice for the main crop.

Monarch

A modern celeriac with pale flesh and comparatively smooth roots. A useful addition for easier preparation in the kitchen.

Asterix F1

An early hybrid producing large, round roots for autumn harvesting and storage. Useful bolting resistance helps support a dependable crop.

Giant Prague

A long-established celeriac with large roots. Retain as a heritage alternative where seed cost and traditional varieties matter.

Key risks
Slugs

Slugs can damage seedlings and later chew holes in swollen roots.

Carrot fly

Brown lines or tunnels across the lower part of the root may be caused by carrot root fly maggots.

Frost

Celeriac is hardy, but exposed roots and frozen ground can make winter harvesting difficult.

Celery fly (leaf miner)

Celery leaf miner makes pale blotches that turn brown and papery.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
40
ROOT CROPS

Keep growth steady from the start.

Cold or drought checks can reduce the crop and encourage bolting.

Keep the crown at soil level.

Celeriac needs no celery-style earthing up or blanching.

Sowing & planting
Surface sow
Grow on
Keep the crown clear
Sow indoors 

Scatter the tiny seed over moist compost and barely cover it. Keep it moist and allow up to three weeks for germination.

Prick out 

Move small seedlings into individual modules. Keep them growing steadily, sheltered from cold and drought. Harden off before planting.

Plant out 

Set the swollen stem-base level with the soil. Firm and water well. Keep soil and mulch clear of the crown.

Soil & preparation
Use rich, moisture-retentive soil with plenty of well-rotted compost. Improved heavier ground often suits shallow-rooted celeriac.
Mulch to conserve moisture; add an appropriate organic feed only if the soil lacks fertility.
Looking after the crop
Weed until the leaves meet. Water in dry weather and mulch with compost to protect the shallow roots.
Keep soil and mulch off the crown. Remove side shoots and damaged or horizontal outer leaves. Keep healthy upright foliage.
Harvesting & storage
On well-drained soil, leave sound roots in place under straw in cold spells. On wet sites lift in autumn before waterlogging.
Loosen roots with a spade or trowel, then lift and trim lightly. Store cool in moist coir or peat-free compost and check for decay.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Slugs	Seedlings chewed; holes in mature roots.	Check and hand-pick; lift damaged roots before rot develops.
Carrot fly	Brown tunnels in the swollen base.	Use insect mesh; avoid damage during weeding.
Frost	Frost damage on exposed bases.	Use straw in cold spells; lift and store on wet or exposed sites.
Celery fly (leaf miner)	Pale blotch mines in leaves.	Tolerate light damage; remove badly mined leaf parts.
Bolting	Flower stems replace root growth.	Avoid cold and drought checks; harden off gradually.
Celery leaf spot (blight)	Brown spots spread through leaves.	Use healthy seed; remove affected leaves and avoid splashing.
Hollow or holed roots	Internal hollows or pest holes.	Keep moisture even; inspect and discard rotten tissue.
Damping off	Seedlings rot at the base and fall.	Use clean compost, water less and ventilate.
Woodlice	Woodlice in existing root holes.	Check for slugs or rot. Lift sound parts promptly.
Final tips

Fleece can help newly planted seedlings establish; keep them growing without cold or dry checks.

Check stored roots regularly and remove any that begin to rot.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
